Abstract:Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging.

roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts.
Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally.
One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons.
Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model.
These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods.
Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions.
This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method.
Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

The Short Version
I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.
After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared.
The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread.
What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning.
This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them.
Neural networks are already clean.
There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability.
The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations.
The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.
The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots.

At a high-level, some of my biggest concerns are:
- Refuting a non-standard definition of superposition.
A major theme of the essay is refuting superposition.
But all the arguments in the essay only work for the highly non-standard definition of superposition in the essay.
In particular, the essay defines superposition as “unrelated features” being grouped in the same neuron,22 “Superposition: a change in learning principle where the network packs unrelated things into the same neurons because they rarely collide.” (Superposition of the Gaps) and presents this as the original meaning from the circuits thread (see Concern 2 for more discussion around how the circuits thread actually defined superposition).
Grouping unrelated features is a phenomenon that can follow from superposition, but I’m not aware of anyone treating it as a definition, and theoretical models of superposition only predict it in certain conditions.
In other conditions, the opposite can happen, with superposition grouping similar features.
- Reproduction Differences.
When I’ve tried to replicate Nick’s experiments, or run the standard experiments for some of the empirical claims, my results have been different than those described.
This has been true even for basic experiments where it’s hard to imagine errors.
- Mischaracterising other papers.
In several cases, other papers (including my own) are described inaccurately.
I don’t think any of this is done in malice or with bad intentions.
It seems like there may be sincere misunderstandings.
I’m also conscious that Nick’s post isn’t the final scientific paper, which is still forthcoming.
Concern 1: Neuron Explanations do not Stand Up to Standard Experiments
The essay argues that the field’s canonical examples of polysemanticity in vision models were misinterpreted.
On its account, the cat-and-car neuron is really a V detector, and the car circuit’s dog-and-car readers are really generalised pose neurons, so neither is evidence that neurons mix unrelated things.
These explanations make concrete predictions, and the research community has developed a lot of tools for evaluating precisely these kinds of claims.
In this section, I’ll use some of the standard battery.
For each section, I’ll check:
- what the neuron responds to across its whole activation range, not just the top
- where possible, whether it responds to clean synthetic versions of the hypothesised stimulus
- which parts of an image it depends on, by covering them up
- whether the upstream neurons that should feed it actually do
- what downstream neurons use it for
None of these tools rely on any special frame, on superposition, or on whether “features” are the right way to think about things.
They’re basic empirical tests that I believe s
[...]
ks, while the note is built on features (see also Appendix: How much does defining “feature” matter?).
The idea of features being the wrong thing to try to understand is a reasonable position to hold, but it means it is wrong to cite this note as support.
Concern 5: Not a mechanistic explanation
One final concern is higher level.
Recursive generalisation is a theory of what we should expect to see group together under the same neuron.
I’d understand it as a theory of learning dynamics and superposition structure.
But I’m not sure how it provides a path to mechanistic explanation.
That is, I’m not sure how recursive generalisation helps me understand how a neural network computes its output from the input.
Suppose we look at a polysemantic neuron and realise that it’s actually linked by a tree of associations to one original concept.
But if the different concepts grouped together are actually used by the downstream network, they still need be distinguished somehow (presumably by other neurons?), leaving open the hard question superposition was trying to address.
Conclusion
None of this settles whether neural networks are “already clean,” and there’s a lot in the essay I haven’t touched.
However, I don’t think what’s discussed here is minor.
For example, the cat-and-car neuron and the car circuit are where the essay says the original evidence “fell.” The things I looked at don’t survive what I consider quite basic checks.
That matters beyond these examples.
Much of the essay’s other evidence comes from models and data readers can’t inspect, where the same method has to be taken on trust.
Of course, they might very well be correct, but I do think we should avoid updating too much on the results of the paper until such checks can be run.
The non-standard definition of superposition also has pervasive effects throughout the essay, and the idea that the superposition hypothesis was wrong is likely the most important takeaway.
I really regret having to have this conversation in public like this.
If not for the intense public interest, the level of media attention, the quickly moving environment, and the potentially high safety stakes, I would have preferred to provide more opportunity for private dialogue first.
But I think there’s an important public interest argument in responding quickly in this case.

The Pitch
Last week Nick Cammarata, writing for Goodfire, made a bold and genuinely exciting claim: neural networks are “already clean.” Roughly 90% of the neurons in a modern model like Qwen3-32B have one job — a single, nameable concept — and the old story about “superposition” (networks cramming many features into each neuron) was mostly a story about bad microscopes, not messy networks.
If true, mechanistic interpretability just got a lot more tractable.
You could read a model the way you read a codebase.
We wanted it to be true.
So we ran the test it deserves.
A quick note on the "we": there's no lab here.
It's me and my AI research assistant — a two-person shop, one of us silicon.
We did this overnight, on a home PC
Over one evening, on a CPU, for $7.74 in API calls, we reproduced the core measurement on Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B — with three controls the essay doesn’t report.
The headline control is embarrassingly simple: run the exact same pipeline on an untrained, randomly-initialized network.
If the method calls random noise “clean” too, the method is measuring itself, not the model.
Here is what we found, in one sentence: the labeller called 84% of pure-noise neurons “one job,” versus 52% of real ones — and neither set could predict its own behavior.
The specimen might be clean.
But the microscope is fogged, and this time it’s not the architecture’s fault.
It’s the labels.
Part 1: What the Essay Actually Claims
Cammarata’s argument is a four-step reinterpretation of a decade of interpretability folklore:
- Networks use one learning principle (recursive generalization), not two (generalization plus superposition).
- Better architectures and better visualization tools make neurons far more interpretable than the 2020-era “Zoom In” work suggested.
- Understanding compounds — once you label a few neurons, their neighbors get easier (the crossword effect).
- So “this might be most of what we need,” and interpretability might be far more tractable than the field assumes.
The empirical spine is a labelling procedure: show a strong LLM a neuron’s top-activating text snippets, ask it to name the neuron’s “job,” and tag the result one job / two related jobs / unclear.
On Qwen3-32B, Cammarata reports a split of roughly 90% / 7% / 3%.
Ninety percent one job.
Hence: already cle
[...]
hat separates “the label describes the peak” from “the label describes the neuron.”
Then the three controls:
- Random directions.
Run the identical pipeline on 300 random unit vectors in the same activation space.
If random directions score like neurons, the neuron basis isn’t special — the labelling method just makes anything sound meaningful.
- Random-init network.
The same architecture with untrained weights.
This is the floor: how legible does pure, structureless noise look?
- Explanation-swap null.
Score a neuron’s snippets using a different neuron’s label.
If that scores above zero, the “signal” is an artifact of the scorer, not the explanation.
Everything was pre-registered before we saw a single number.
Models from different families for explainer and scorer.
Every datapoint computed from data on disk; no estimated numbers.
Part 3: What Broke
Finding 1 — the labels describe only the peak (critique a: confirmed).
Trained neurons do predict their extreme top activations: r = 0.26, and that signal is real — swap in a random other neuron’s label and it collapses to 0.002.
But move one step down the distribution and it’s gone: r = 0.09 at the top-1% band, 0.02 at 1–10%, and 0.00 at 10–50%.
Zero neurons out of 299 cleared our pre-registered legibility bar (top-1% r ≥ 0.5 and 1–10% r ≥ 0.3).
SwiGLU neurons are so heavy-tailed — median peak-to-std of 46 — that the literal “top 1%” of activations is mostly small values nowhere near the peaks the label describes.
Finding 2 — the labeller calls anything “one job” (critique b: confirmed).
This is the result that should change how the field reads labelling studies.
Our explainer tagged 84% of untrained, random-init neurons as “one job” — more than the 52% it gave real trained neurons — while those random-init labels simulate at r = 0.01.
The label class carries almost no information about measured legibility.
Worse: among real neurons, the ones tagged “unclear” actually scored better at the peaks (r = 0.33) than the ones tagged “one job” (0.23).
A 90/7/3 split is not evidence of clean networks if 84/7/9 is what you get from noise.
Finding 3 — the labels don’t predict behavior (the causal test the essay skips).
We took 50 neurons, had the model predict (from each label alone) which tokens the neuron should influence, froze those predictions to disk, then ablated (×0) and amplified (×3) each neuron.
The result: 0 o
[...]
odels — the whole structure rests on whether the checkers are calibrated.
A verifier that says “clean” 84% of the time on pure noise isn’t a safety layer.
It’s a liability with a confident voice.
The Takeaways
- Neurons are a real unit, but “already clean” overshoots.
Legibility is confined to the extreme activation peak; below it, the labels say nothing.
- Never trust a labelling study without a noise floor.
Random-init neurons got labelled “one job” 84% of the time.
Counts of plausible labels are not evidence.
- Make interpretability a calibrated verifier.
Per-band simulation scores, a random-init control, and a causal test are cheap, and they’re the difference between measuring the model and measuring the microscope.
The specimen may well be clean.
We just can’t tell yet — and the tool that said we could was reading noise as signal.

What Makes a Neural Net Clean
Every acquisition changes what a neural network learns next.
But if neural circuitry itself is a moving target, what learned structure is actually conserved?
In Neural Networks Are Already Clean, Nick Cammarata notes the importance of identifying when mechanisms are used in later development.
When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects.
I mean that a network’s parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers.1
Cammarata follows a neuron in a retrained InceptionV1 model whose strongest responses initially come from yellow-flower images, some with dogs.
Green objects and dogs without flowers appear later, followed by broccoli.
This developmental history traces how a mechanism’s responses branch into related domains.
Cammarata calls the branching of responses across related inputs “recursive generalization.”
Cammarata traces how a mechanism develops.
Training targets determine what counts as successful downstream use.
Building on this idea, I ask how learning preserves useful capabilities while the circuitry changes.
My experiments test whether responses persist and downstream readers continue to depend on them.
One path leads to another
In Cammarata’s circuit-ecology hypothesis, established mechanisms and their readers can learn related tasks faster than competitors starting fresh.
As their predictions improve, less error remains to train competing pathways.
He proposes that repeated reuse can produce recursive generalization.1
Applied to Cammarata’s flower neuron, the hypothesis suggests a possible mechanism.
A flower-responsive neuron might also respond weakly to vegetation.
Training on green objects could strengthen that response into a green signal for a later broccoli detector.
Learning green could therefore make broccoli responsiveness easier to acquire.
A broccoli detector that uses the green signal would give the earlier mechanism a new role.
This is the causal interpretation explored below, rather than a measured dependency in Cammarata’s flower neuron.
A reader is a downstream computation that uses the output of a specific pathway.
I built a synthetic model to test when an earlier acquisition helps later learning and when it becomes a constraint.2 The model receives binary flower, green, and texture cues.
Supplying these distinctions directly lets us study how feature use develops without explaining a mechanism’s initial discovery.
The broccoli task requires green and texture together.
Flower discrimination means correctly classifying inputs with and without the flower cue, even when response strength changes.
I measure learning pressure as the negative loss gradient on a parameter.
For ordinary gradient descent, its sign and magnitude determine the proposed update per unit learning rate.
Constraints can also alter the update.
A shared capacity limit, for example, can weaken flower responsiveness without a direct flower-loss gradient.
In the first experiment, I trained two readers to predict a green-dependent target using competing pathways.
Training updates both the feature coefficients and the weights readers use to combine those features.

At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks.

Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith.
Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias.
When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says.
“Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”
But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place.
“Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says.
“And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”
Back to cars and cats
Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1.
“I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says.
But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around.
Take the car-and-cat neuron.
Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.
It hit him: It was a V shape.
“I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says.
“But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently.

A central challenge is choosing the units over which we trace these computations.
Neurons are the simplest option, but many researchers believe they don't form a sparse or clean basis: individual “features” are often spread across many neurons [9, 10].
This has motivated a range of learned alternatives: sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [11, 12], transcoders [13, 14, 8], or directly training the model to have sparse circuits [15].
These learned feature bases are powerful, but they also come with drawbacks.
They only approximate the original model, which introduces hard-to-interpret error terms [16, 17].
Their features can split or merge in unintuitive ways, making them unstable and often polysemantic [12, 18].
And because they must be retrained as the model evolves, they are expensive to apply throughout training [19].
For these reasons, it is valuable to extract as much interpretability as we can directly from the neuron basis, even if individual neurons are not always as cleanly interpretable as learned sparse features [11].
This motivates a natural question: Are neuron-level circuits really as unsparse as previously believed?
Our work revisits this assumption.
Surprisingly, we find that circuits built directly in the neuron basis can be just as sparse and faithful as circuits built from SAE features.

The cool star in the T Corona Borealis system is a swollen red giant.
It continually transfers material to its companion in the system, the hot star.
The hot star is a white dwarf, surrounded by an accretion disk made of material transferred over from the other star.

The constellation Corona Borealis (the Northern Crown) is home to one of the most anticipated objects in modern observational astronomy: T Coronae Borealis (T CrB).
Unlike most novae, which are observed only once in human history, T CrB is a recurrent nova.
With a period of approximately 80 years, the system is currently on the verge of a new outburst, following its well-documented eruptions in 1866 and 1946.
The Binary System: An Unequal Pair
T CrB is not a single star but a close binary system consisting of a red giant and an extremely dense white dwarf.
These two objects orbit each other at such a short distance that a continuous mass transfer occurs.
The red giant sheds matter from its outer layers, which accumulates in an accretion disk around the white dwarf.
Due to the intense gravity of the white dwarf, this material – primarily hydrogen – is compressed and heated.
When the pressure and temperature on the surface of the white dwarf reach a critical threshold, a thermonuclear runaway occurs.
This violent explosion ejects the accumulated matter into space, causing the system to brighten by a factor of thousands within just a few hours.
Historical Context: 1866 and 1946
The history of T Coronae Borealis (T CrB) is exceptionally well-recorded.
During both known outbursts, the system reached a peak apparent magnitude of approximately 2.0 mag.
At this brightness, T CrB was clearly visible to the naked eye, rivaling Polaris (the North Star) in luminosity.
A characteristic feature of this nova is its extremely steep rise in brightness followed by a rapid decline.
Historically, T CrB often exhibits a secondary maximum several months after the initial peak, making it a target of great interest for long-term photometric monitoring.
Current Status: The “Pre-Eruption Dip”
Why are astronomers worldwide focused on this star right now?
Observations show that prior to the 1946 outburst, T CrB underwent a significant drop in brightness, known as a “pre-eruption dip.” An identical phenomenon has been documented since early 2023.
This deviation from its quiescent brightness is considered one of the most reliable indicators that the thermonuclear process on the surface is nearing its ignition point.
Currently, T Coronae Boreealis (T CrB) remains in its quiescent phase at approximately 10.0 – 11.0 mag, making it a target for binoculars and telescopes including cameras.
However, once the eruption begins, it will briefly become one of the brightest objects in the spring and summer sky.
Observation Details
T CrB is located in the constellation Corona Borealis, a distinctive semicircle of stars between Bootes and Hercules.

No significant increase in brightness has been reported yet.
Photometric monitoring is ongoing.
Outlook
T Coronae Borealis offers a rare opportunity to witness a stellar catastrophe in real-time.
For the scientific community, this outburst is crucial for understanding the dynamics of mass transfer and the physical conditions on the surfaces of white dwarfs.
For amateur astronomers, it promises to be one of the most spectacular celestial events of the decade.

The predicted eruption of T Coronae Borealis (T CrB) will likely be one of the most exciting astronomical events in recent memory.
If it mirrors the 1946 eruption, T CrB could brighten from V~9.8 to V~1.7 in less than 24 hours, then gradually return to its pre-eruption brightness over the next 45 days.
Shortly thereafter, it may brighten again to V~8, staying bright for about two months before setting back to its usual state.
To capture this event, preparation is key – and the AAVSO is here to help.
Whether you’re a casual stargazer or an experienced observer, we have valuable advice for you.
If you’d like to help AAVSO record this event for its scientific value, please pay close attention to the details below.
During the eruption, we will request visual photometry, multi-color optical photometry (all bands), and near-infrared photometry (JH bands).
We will also request spectroscopic observation at low resolution and focused high-resolution observations of specific spectral lines.
Due to the rapid nature of this event and potential for flares and other transient phenomena, we ask that photometric observers either (a) observe continuously in a single photometric filter, or (b) cycle through as many standard photometric filters as possible while maintaining good calibration.
The AAVSO recommends that observers practice observing both T CrB and Alf CrB in advance to learn how their equipment performs at the extreme brightness ranges anticipated for T CrB.
Note: T CrB will reach solar conjunction in late November, making it extremely difficult or nearly impossible to observe safely due to its proximity to the Sun.
If you attempt to observe during this time, please exercise extreme caution.
Stargazers
If you are a stargazer looking to witness the upcoming eruption of T CrB, we encourage you to do the following things to prepare.
Download a copy of the AAVSO star chart for T CrB.
On my chart, I’ve connected the brightest stars in Corona Borealis to make it easier for me to locate T CrB in the sky.
Use the chart to locate T CrB in the sky and go out weekly to keep track of it.
Keep in mind that our view of the sky changes slightly from night-to-night, so you’ll want to go out at least once a week to know where to look.
When the system erupts, consider capturing the moment using a camera.
To produce the best images, use a tripod or other solid object to steady your camera.
I suggest that you take a photo every night to document the system’s dramatic changes in brightness.
While these images may not be scientifically valuable due to JPEG compression, they’ll create lasting memories for you to treasure.
Lastly, I would suggest you consider participating in the Astronomical League’s Special Observing Award on T Crb.
For their level 1 award, you don’t even have to be a member of the Astronomical League.
Visual Observers
Visual observers should prepare for the eruption in advance by printing both A-scale [PDF] and B-scale [PDF] charts covering the range V~ 1.0 – 10.8 in advance.
Visual observers who routinely use telescopes or binoculars are advised that suitable comparison stars may not be located within their FOV.
As such, they should practice observing without binoculars / telescopes or become accustomed to rapid star hopping to obtain suitable comparison stars.
During the eruption, visual observers should collect observations three to four times per night, ideally spaced at least an hour apart.
Please be aware that Alf CrB (star 22) is an eclipsing binary with a 17 day period and 13-hour eclipse of depth 0.1 mag.
Observers should make independent estimates of T CrB using both the 22 and 28 stars when T CrB is at its maximum brightness.

PEP observations will be critical to establish T CrB’s behavior during the brightest phases of the eruption.
PEP observers should prepare for the eruption in advance by printing both A-scale charts covering the range V~ 1.0 – 10.8 in advance [PDF] and referencing the corresponding UBVRIJH photometry table [PDF].
They should follow standard observing practices and reduce their data using the PEP data reduction spreadsheet.
During the eruption, PEP observers are encouraged to observe the system as frequently as possible due to the likely presence of flares and other transient events.

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.
While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated.
The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D.
Cook and Beth M.
Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - SEPTEMBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand increased 1.3 percent in September, seasonally
adjusted, the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today.
Final demand prices moved up 0.5
percent in August and 0.2 percent in July.
(See table A.) The September increase is the largest
advance since rising 1.7 percent in March 2022.
On an unadjusted basis, the index for final
demand climbed 6.3 percent for the 12 months ended in September, the largest 12-month
increase since moving up 6.4 percent in December 2022.
In September, prices for final demand goods rose 2.6 percent, and the index for final demand
services advanced 0.8 percent.
Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services moved up 0.5 percent in September
after increasing 0.3 percent in August.
For the 12 months ended in September, the index for final
demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: Prices for final demand goods advanced 2.6 percent in September, the largest
increase since data were first calculated in December 2009.
Over 80 percent of the broad-based rise
in September is attributable to the index for final demand energy, which jumped 10.8 percent.
Prices
for final demand foods and for final demand goods less foods and energy advanced 1.2 percent and
0.3 percent, respectively.
Product detail: Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to
prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent.
The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables,
jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose.
In contrast, prices for chicken eggs
dropped 39.7 percent.
The indexes for thermoplastic resins and materials and for commercial electric
power also declined.
(See table 2.)
Final demand services: Prices for final demand services moved up 0.8 percent in September, the
largest rise since advancing 0.8 percent in April.
Nearly half of the broad-based September increase
can be attributed to a 1.4-percent rise in margins for final demand trade services.
The indexes for
final demand transportation and warehousing services and for final demand services less trade,
transportation, and warehousing also advanced, 3.4 percent and 0.3 percent, respectively.
Product detail: Over 20 percent of the September increase in prices for final demand services can be
traced to margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling, which advanced 3.9 percent.
The indexes
for truck transportation of freight, food and alcohol wholesaling, traveler accommodation services,
food retailing, and airline passenger services also rose.
Conversely, margins for automotive fuels and
lubricants retailing dropped 30.3 percent.
